paper_topic: Cap-and-Spill: two-pass CUDA-graph-compatible MoE dispatch using quantile-based buffer capacity

nodes.text: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have emerged as a powerful paradigm for scaling neural networks efficiently (Shazeer et al., 2017; Lepikhin et al., 2020; Fedus et al., 2021).
By activating only a subset of experts for each input token, MoE architectures achieve the capacity of dense models at a fraction of the computational cost.

Recent models such as Mixtral (Jiang et al., 2024a) and DeepSeek-V2 (Shao et al., 2024) have demonstrated state-of-the-art performance using this approach, driving widespread adoption in production systems.

A critical component of distributed MoE inference is the dispatch phase, where tokens are redistributed across GPUs via AllToAll collective communication to reach their assigned experts (Hwang et al., 2022; Rajbhandari et al., 2022).
nodes.display_label: Dispatch via AllToAll in MoE inference

nodes.text: CUDA graphs have become essential for high-throughput inference, as they eliminate kernel launch overhead by capturing and replaying sequences of GPU operations.

However, CUDA graphs require all buffer sizes to be fixed at capture time, creating a fundamental tension with the dynamic nature of MoE routing: current approaches must allocate buffers for the worst-case token count across all peer pairs, leading to substantial padding waste.
Our analysis of Mixtral-8x7B routing traces reveals that this worst-case allocation is highly inefficient.
The maximum per-peer token count (Cmax = 43) is 8.4× larger than the mean count (5.1), resulting in 88% padding overhead.
However, the distribution is heavy-tailed: 99% of per-peer counts fall below C = 16, suggesting that smaller buffers could handle the vast majority of dispatch operations.
We propose Cap-and-Spill, a two-pass dispatch strategy that exploits this statistical property while maintaining CUDA-graph compatibility.
The first pass uses quantile-based buffer capacity (C = Q99 ) to handle most tokens efficiently; the second pass dispatches overflow tokens that exceed the capacity.
Both passes use fixed buffer sizes, enabling full CUDA-graph capture.
Counterintuitively, we find that unconditionally executing both passes outperforms conditional execution by eliminating synchronization overhead.
We propose Cap-and-Spill, a two-pass CUDA-graph-compatible MoE dispatch algorithm that uses quantile-based buffer capacity to reduce padding waste while handling overflow tokens in a second pass.

We demonstrate 33.9% mean latency reduction (1077 µs → 712 µs) on 8×A100 NVLink with Mixtral-8x7B routing traces, recovering 53.2% of the gap to oracle eager dispatch while maintaining exact correctness.

We characterize the heavy-tailed nature of MoE routing distributions (Cmax /µ = 8.4×) and show that the 99th percentile provides the optimal operating point, balancing buffer reduction (2.69×) with minimal overflow (5.4%).

observations:
FA0201 follows a tight problem-solution arc framing CUDA-graph buffer padding waste in MoE dispatch. Para 1 (N1-N4) is pure Context: MoE as scaling paradigm, sparse activation, production adoption (Mixtral, DeepSeek-V2), and dispatch via AllToAll. Para 2 introduces the only genuine Prior_Work / Limitation pair: N5 (CUDA graphs are essential for throughput) is reversed by N6 ('However, CUDA graphs require fixed buffer sizes... worst-case... padding waste'), where the 'current approaches' clause names the prior practice being critiqued. The Limitation N6 thus has Prior_Work N5 as its required upstream source.

Para 3 (N7-N9) is empirical Result content that analyzes Mixtral routing traces and provides quantitative justification for the method's premise — Cmax/mean = 8.4x with 88% padding waste, and a heavy-tailed distribution where 99% of counts fall below C=16. The intra-paragraph 'However' (N8 -> N9) is a contrast between the worst-case-vs-mean ratio and the heavy-tail observation that motivates the proposed quantile-based buffer.

The Method block (N10-N13) decomposes Cap-and-Spill into the two-pass strategy, fixed buffers for graph capture, and the counterintuitive unconditional execution finding. Three Contribution nodes (C1-C3) close the intro and each maps via an addresses edge back to the single Limitation N6 (the worst-case padding waste being resolved). N13 is a fork node (out_degree=3 to C1/C2/C3); N6 is the join target of the three addresses back-edges. No anchor paper — this is a pure systems contribution rather than a derivative of one prior method.
